{{< include _compose-kit.qmd >}}

A **motif** is a short musical idea, often only three to six notes, that a piece keeps coming back to. It is recognised by its rhythm and its shape
more than by its exact notes, so it can change and still be heard as the same idea. That is what **developing** a motif means: changing it
step by step so the music grows out of one idea instead of jumping from one new idea to the next.

The best-known example is the opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony: three short notes and one long one. The whole first movement is
built from that rhythm, on different notes, in different instruments, louder and softer.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="108"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Beethoven, Symphony No. 5: the opening, one line (the whole orchestra plays it in octaves)
M:2/4
L:1/8
Q:1/4=108
K:Cm
z G G G | !fermata!E4 | z F F F | D4- | !fermata!D4 |]
</script></div>

**How to use the page.** Each technique below has a short example: the motif, then the change. The motif is always the same one,
**C E G E** with the rhythm *short short short long*, so you can hear what each change does to it.

## The techniques

### Repetition

Play it again, exactly. It sounds simple, but a listener needs to hear an idea twice before it sticks. Most motifs are repeated straight away.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, then repetition
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C E G E4 z | C E G E4 z |]
</script></div>

### Sequence

The same shape, starting on a different note: usually a step higher or lower each time. Sequences make the music feel like it is moving
somewhere. In a **diatonic** sequence the notes stay in the key, so the steps between them may change size slightly (a major third becomes a minor one).

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, then two steps up the scale
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C E G E4 z | D F A F4 z | E G B G4 z |]
</script></div>

### Inversion

Turn it upside down. Each step up becomes the same step down. The rhythm stays the same, so it is still recognisable.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, then its inversion (from the same first note)
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
c e g e4 z | c A F A4 z |]
</script></div>

### Retrograde

Play it backwards: the last note first. Retrograde is harder to hear than the others, so composers often use it as a hidden link rather than
an obvious one.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, then its retrograde (notes and rhythm backwards)
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C E G E4 z | z E4 G E C |]
</script></div>

### Augmentation and diminution

Make every note twice as long (augmentation) or half as long (diminution). Augmentation sounds broader and more serious: it is a common way to
end a piece. Diminution sounds more urgent.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, augmentation, diminution
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C E G E4 z | C2 E2 G2 E2- | E6 z2 | C/E/G/E2 z/ z4 |]
</script></div>

### Fragmentation

Use only part of it: the first two or three notes, repeated or sequenced on their own. Breaking an idea into pieces speeds the music up.
It is how the continuation of a sentence works (see [Composing 1](compose-melody.qmd#the-sentence)).

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Motif, then fragments of its first three notes, going up
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C E G E4 z | C E G D F A E G | B c4 z3 |]
</script></div>

### Changing one thing at a time

You can also keep the rhythm and change the notes, keep the notes and change the rhythm, change the harmony under it, the instrument, the
register, the dynamics, or the articulation. The rule that keeps it recognisable: **change one or two things, keep the rest**.

## The motif lab

Pick a motif or type your own. Then build a phrase: each button adds a changed copy of the last group. Start with **Motif**, then try,
for example, *Repeat, Sequence up, Fragment, Fragment, Land on C*. Play it and decide what to keep. **Copy ABC** gives the phrase in
ABC, which the [Notation page](/tools/notation.qmd) opens (paste it into its ABC box).

<div class="cp-try">
<div class="cp-motif"></div>
</div>

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>Explore, then choose.</strong> Make three different phrases from the same motif before you pick one. Copy each into your process
journal with one line on what you changed and how it sounds. That record of trying several ideas and choosing between them is exactly what
MYP Criterion B asks you to show: see [Process 2](process-crit-b.qmd).
</div>

## Listen for it

Motifs are everywhere once you listen for them. A few to try (find a recording, and count how many times you hear the idea):

- **Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, first movement:** the rhythm *short short short long*, in every instrument, all the way through.
- **John Williams, *Jaws*:** two notes a half step apart, alternating, low in the bass. Almost nothing but repetition, and it works.
- **A song's chorus hook:** in most pop songs the hook is a motif, repeated several times in each chorus.
